hook.line: The year the naturalist Linnaeus noted the rules of “tablut” on his Lapland journey. Without that record, the Viking game would still be a mystery.
hook.say: Let’s set sail for the Viking board!

ch.t: The board of the Viking king
ch.say: It travelled far across the sea.
p: Tafl games were widely played in Viking-age Scandinavia. “Hnefatafl” is usually translated “king’s table”.
Carried by ship to Ireland and Britain, it faded from the 12th century as chess took over.

tl: Tafl games said to be played in the North
Researchers reconstruct the rules; modern tournaments follow

ch.say: The defenders must lead the king to a corner.
ch.cap: 11×11 board: king in the centre, 12 defenders, 24 attackers
p: Attackers have numbers; defenders escort the king — an uneven battle is the heart of it.
Pieces move any distance orthogonally and are captured by sandwiching between two.

cards: A giant 19×19 board survives in a medieval manuscript

ch.say: Pieces have even been found in graves.
cards: The naturalist who popularised scientific names for living things — and even jotted down game rules in his travel diary
Gaming pieces, including a king, have been found buried in Viking graves
